title: Is a four-day week the future of work?
text:
Imagine finishing work on Thursday afternoon and having a three-day weekend every week – without earning less money. For a growing number of employees around the world, this is no longer just a dream. In the last few years, many companies have tested a four-day working week, and some of them have decided to keep it.

The idea is simple: people work fewer hours, but they are expected to get the same amount of work done. Supporters say this is possible because tired workers are not very productive. With an extra day off, employees can rest, spend time with their families, do sport or deal with personal matters such as doctor's appointments. As a result, they come back to work with more energy and concentrate better.

Companies that have tried it often report that their staff are happier and less stressed, and that fewer people take sick days or leave for other jobs. Some managers also say that meetings have become shorter, because everybody knows there is less time to waste.

However, the four-day week does not work for everyone. In hospitals, schools or shops, someone has to be there five, six or even seven days a week. For these organisations, giving everybody an extra day off would mean employing more people, which is expensive. Some workers also say that squeezing five days of work into four makes their days long and stressful.

Experts agree that there is no single solution. Perhaps the most important lesson from the experiments is that the traditional nine-to-five, five-day week is not the only way to organise our working lives.
